title: A cloud like a pine tree
saying: nōn alia magis arbor quam pīnus expresserit
author: Pliny the Younger
setting: Misenum, on the Bay of Naples, AD 79

edition.name: Pliny the Younger, Epistulae, Latin text of the Perseus Digital Library (Tufts University), TEI file phi1318.phi001.perseus-lat1 in the PerseusDL canonical-latinLit repository ("Letters", released 2004-08-24); the file's own header names no source edition (its imprint fields are empty), so the editor and year cannot be stated. Checked word for word against The Latin Library's text (thelatinlibrary.com/pliny.ep6.html), which also names no editor

source_text: Nubes - incertum procul intuentibus ex quo monte; Vesuvium fuisse postea cognitum est - oriebatur, cuius similitudinem et formam non alia magis arbor quam pinus expresserit. Nam longissimo velut trunco elata in altum quibusdam ramis diffundebatur, credo quia recenti spiritu evecta, dein senescente eo destituta aut etiam pondere suo victa in latitudinem vanescebat, candida interdum, interdum sordida et maculosa prout terram cineremve sustulerat.
excerpt_note: The second sentence of 6.16.5 and all of 6.16.6. The Perseus file prints the dashes around the parenthesis as spaced hyphens ( - ), and they are kept as printed; The Latin Library prints the same words with long dashes.

translation: A cloud was rising (to people watching from a distance it was unclear from which mountain; afterwards it was learned to have been Vesuvius) whose likeness and shape no other tree would have captured better than a pine. For it was carried up high as if on a very long trunk and then spread out into a kind of branches, I suppose because a fresh blast had lifted it and then, as the blast died down, it was left without support, or was even beaten down by its own weight, and thinned out sideways; at times it was white, at times dirty and blotched, depending on whether it had carried up earth or ash.
translation_note: Pliny writes as an observer at Misenum, across the bay: the parenthesis (incertum ... cōgnitum est) admits that at the time no one knew which mountain it was. expresserit is a potential subjunctive ("would have expressed"). crēdō marks the explanation of the shape as Pliny's own guess. -ve on cineremve means "or" (terram cineremve: "earth or ash").

essay.t: Pliny the Younger wrote this letter to the historian Tacitus, who had asked for an account of his uncle's death to hand down more truthfully to posterity.
Britannica describes Tacitus' Histories as covering AD 69 to 96, a span that includes the eruption.
Only the first four books and part of the fifth survive, reaching AD 70, so whatever Tacitus made of the letter is lost (Wikipedia, a tertiary source).

Pliny's uncle, Pliny the Elder, commanded the fleet at Misenum; the letter dates the first sight of the cloud to the ninth day before the Kalends of September (24 August), when Pliny's mother pointed it out.
The elder Pliny launched warships to bring help, steered toward the danger while dictating notes on what he saw, and died on the shore at Stabiae; his body was found unharmed when daylight returned.
His nephew suggests that dense fumes blocked his breathing, but he marks this as his own inference (ut ego colligo).

The pine-tree image entered science: the US Geological Survey calls large explosive eruptions that build enormous columns of tephra and gas "Plinian", after Pliny the Younger's careful description of Vesuvius.
The USGS puts the death toll at roughly 2,000 people.

In 2018 excavators in Regio V found a charcoal note dated the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November (17 October), with no year; the site's team called it highly probable that it was written a week before an October eruption.

In the Pompeii park's e-journal in 2024, Gabriel Zuchtriegel and colleagues report that charcoal writing put on the same wall on 17 October 2023 was still legible ten months later, so the 2018 note could date from October 78.
They also cite Pedar Foss's 2022 collation of the manuscripts, which found no manuscript support for any date except 24 August.
They do not call August proven: they ask whether archaeology now offers enough to doubt it, and leave the question open.
My summary: August rests on one textual tradition that could be mistaken, October on suggestive but imprecise finds.

questions.q: Why did Pliny write this letter?
options: Tacitus asked for an account of his uncle's death for his history
He was reporting to the emperor as fleet commander
He wanted to publish a scientific treatise on volcanoes
His mother asked him to record the date

questions.q: What does the word crēdō signal in the description of the cloud's shape?
options: That the explanation is Pliny's own guess
That an eyewitness told him so
That he read it in his uncle's notes
That it was common knowledge at Misenum

questions.q: What did the 2023 experiment at Pompeii show about the charcoal note found in 2018?
options: Charcoal writing can stay legible for ten months, so the note could date from October 78
The note must have been written in the week before the eruption
The note was a modern forgery
Charcoal fades within days, so the eruption must have been in October
